extracted.intended_audience: philosophers and historians of mathematics, advanced geometers, and readers interested in the epistemology/practice of Euclidean diagram use
extracted.subtask_description: Reconstructing and explicating the standards for reading, producing, and controlling Euclidean geometric diagrams so they can legitimately contribute to inference; addresses what may be read off a diagram, what must be supplied by discursive text, and how diagrams are disciplined and probed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directly attributable features (three conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directly attributable features are ones with (a) certain explicit perceptual cues that are (b) fairly stable across a range of variation of diagram (‘co-exact’ rather than ‘exact’) and (c) not readily eliminable by diagram discipline, i.e. proper exercise of skill in producing (still imperfect) diagrams required by the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three conditions together delimit what may legitimately be read off a diagram. Examples: region inclusions or intersection points that persist under reasonable perturbation of the drawing. Anti-pattern: reading off visually fragile equalities or straightness that would disappear under slight variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance/topology of a diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance or topology of a diagram comprises the inclusions and contiguities of regions, segments, and points in the diagram (strictly speaking, only insofar as not eliminable by diagram discipline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat appearance as a topological datum (who contains what, what touches what, ordering on lines, two-place intersections). This topology largely determines the diagram's attributable (co-exact) features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to regions (explicit perceptual cue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek/Euclidean practice treats diagrams as made up primarily of regions (schema) rather than the delimiting curves; a 'figure' is that which is contained by boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading traditional geometric diagrams, focus on delimited planar regions and their relations rather than treating curves as primary. Example: Euclid's circle is a plane figure contained by one line, not simply the curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary recognitions sanctioned by practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional practice recognizes bounded regions or extended objects (line segments, triangles, angles), containment relationships (part–whole, point-in-region, line-in-region), and intersections of two (but not more) curves as primary recognitions from diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only recognize those objects/relations that are supported by the diagram as produced and/or by stipulation in the text. Examples and edge-cases from Proclus (e.g. four-sided triangle, exterior angle) show that some things require explicit stipulation before being referenced in proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for equality and inequality from diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of equality/inequality read from a diagram require the most explicit possible form (coincidence arising directly from diagram constraints); indirect visual equalities are not allowed to be read off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equalities permitted from diagrams are those realized by direct coincidence (e.g. a common side). Inequalities may be read only when realized as proper inclusions; otherwise equality/inequality must be derived from the discursive text. Example: Euclid I.20 is proved rather than assumed from appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact vs co-exact attribution (fundamental distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-exact attributes: conditions unaffected by a range of continuous variations of a specified diagram (topological/inequality-type features). Exact attributes: conditions that survive only in isolated diagrams under perturbation (straightness, equality of angles, exact proportionalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-exact attributes may be legitimately read off the diagram; exact attributes may not be read off and must be licensed by prior discursive stipulation (postulates, definitions). Use this distinction to explain and block typical 'fallacies of diagram use' that assume exact conditions from appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of exact attributes and their licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact attributes include straightness of lines, equality of angles or segments, congruence, proportionality, con-cyclicity, tangency, parallelism, and three-or-more-point intersections. These are unstable under perturbation and therefore must be licensed by prior discursive text entries (definitions/postulates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact attributions license powerful algebraic/equational inferences (transitivity, substitution, proportionality manipulations) and so carry strict justificatory requirements: they should appear in the text (e.g. Postulate 3 for circles) rather than be read off the diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-exact attributes as topology (what may be indicated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-exact attributions express recognition of regions, segments, points and their inclusions and contiguities: non-empty delimited regions (triangles, squares, circles as regions but not circularity), angles that delimit regions (< two right angles), two-place intersection points, non-parallel lines, non-tangencies, and containment/ordering relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-exact attributions can arise either by stipulation/entry in the discursive text or directly from the diagram; they are 'locally invariant' under allowed variations and so are safe to use in diagram-based inference, subject to diagram discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram discipline (production and refinement standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for proper production and refinement of diagrams implemented by constructing diagrams line-by-line according to stipulations; diagrams are subject to practical quality control though ancient practice lacks fully explicit complete rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructions must be executed so stipulated connectivity is unequivocally readable. If defects in exact attributes or defects that could affect co-exact topology are detectable and improvable, the diagram should be redrawn or rejected. Ancient practice relies on skilled physical production and reﬁnement rather than formal prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control requirements for exact attributes (re-draw/reject conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagram should be re-drawn or rejected if (i) a line said to be straight is so crooked that it can be noticeably improved affecting topology; (ii) outrageous defects in a circle or circle segment are present; (iii) clear failures of alleged equalities are visible; (iv) clear failures of alleged parallelism appear relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These checks concern individual elements (straightness) or relations (equalities, parallelism) and require detection and corrective control targeted to the specific stipulated elements; failure triggers corrective action (redraw) under diagram discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being 'subject to' an exact attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When diagram discipline is in force with respect to an exact claim, the diagram is said to be 'subject to' that exact attribution: it need not display the exact attribute unequivocally, but must be held to standards in relation to its argumentative function and may be replaced if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'subject to' relation focuses quality control on particular stipulations; any explicit co-exact condition that is not eliminable by reﬁnement relative to those exact stipulations will be regarded as indicated and usable in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atypicality control via redrawing and case-examination (not mere genericity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding global 'atypicality' of diagrams by single redrawing is inadequate for co-exact attributes. Traditional practice controls atypicality through redrawing together with disjunctive case examination, and via proposals of cases and objections that probe diagram behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern 'generic diagram' avoidance (redraw until generic) works for exact attributes but not for co-exact/topological properties; one must examine multiple cases and respond to objections to ensure conclusions are robust across allowed diagram variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions: determinateness and uniqueness (practical/grasped standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric constructions purport to give unique outcomes (or finitely many variants) in particular cases; practice expects a non-propositional grasp that executing a construction yields the intended unique outcome (e.g., joining two points by the straight line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniqueness need not always be verbally asserted in Euclid, but is taken as part of constructional control. When constructions pile up, participants may lack intuitive grasp of all eventualities and must either rely on this procedural control or make explicit propositional claims about outcomes and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probing diagram behavior and surveying possible outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because diagram appearance can be extremely sensitive (especially near boundary cases), traditional practice employs probing of diagram behavior and explicit examination of possible cases to detect when small perturbations change topology or the applicability of later constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case-splitting and propositional proofs about possible outcomes to handle sensitive situations (e.g., the 'all triangles are isosceles' fallacy arises from failing to probe alternative diagram behaviors). Probing and objections are part of ancient practice's control mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on what diagramming practice can control
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact stipulations (straight lines, perfect circles) cannot be fully attained; only metric accuracy sufficient to render unequivocally readable co-exact properties associated with further constructions is required and achievable. Complex connectivity requirements may be inscrutable to control by drawing alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when diagram production cannot guarantee required co-exact conditions; then rely on constructions, preliminary results, or propositional case analysis to secure needed attributions. Do not over-attribute from a diagram when control is unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of co-exact equational pitfalls (whole = sum of parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-exact equational conditions (e.g., treating a whole as the sum of visual parts AB = AP + PB) can be equational and so lead to strong (and sometimes erroneous) conclusions if not carefully controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control such attributions via diagram discipline and probing; for near-degenerate or sensitive instances (close-to-isosceles triangles) appearances that suggest equalities of whole and parts may be unstable and must be treated with case distinction or rejected unless adequately secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of letters/labels as an ancient convention (presentation standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling diagram elements (points, lines) with letters to indicate them is an ancient practice and part of conventional diagram presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ labels to identify elements unequivocally in discourse and to anchor stipulations and constructions; while not a philosophical justificatory standard, consistent labeling supports the discursive link between text and diagram.
